name: Ophthalmic nerve (trigeminal V1)
func: The top branch of the trigeminal nerve. It carries touch, pain and temperature from the forehead, scalp, upper eyelid, eye and the top of the nose, and it starts the blink reflex when your eye is touched.

levels.kid:
Your face has a big **feeling nerve** with three branches, like a tree with three limbs. The **ophthalmic nerve** is the **top branch**.

It lets you **feel** things on your **forehead**, your **eyebrows**, your top **eyelids**, the top of your **nose**, and even the front of your **eye**.

If a tiny speck of dust lands on your eye, this nerve notices it right away and sends a fast message to your brain. Your brain makes you **blink** and your eyes make **tears** to wash the dust out. So this nerve is like a security guard for your eyes!
levels.hs:
The **ophthalmic nerve (V1)** is the first and smallest of the three branches of the **trigeminal nerve (CN V)**, the main sensory nerve of the face. The other two are the **maxillary (V2)** and **mandibular (V3)** nerves. V1 is **purely sensory**.

It branches off the **trigeminal ganglion**, which sits in a small pocket of dura (Meckel's cave) near the tip of the petrous temporal bone. V1 runs forward in the **lateral wall of the cavernous sinus**, below CN III and IV, and enters the orbit through the **superior orbital fissure**.

Just before entering the orbit it splits into three branches, easy to remember as **NFL**:
- **Nasociliary**: the eyeball (including the **cornea**), the inside and tip of the nose.
- **Frontal**: becomes the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves to the forehead, scalp and upper eyelid.
- **Lacrimal**: the area near the lacrimal (tear) gland and the outer upper eyelid.

V1 covers skin from the upper eyelid up to roughly the top of the head, and down the bridge of the nose to its tip.
levels.college:
The **nasociliary nerve** enters the orbit inside the **common tendinous ring** and crosses above the optic nerve. Its branches include the **long ciliary nerves** (sensation from the cornea, plus sympathetic fibers to the **dilator pupillae**), a sensory root through the **ciliary ganglion**, the **anterior and posterior ethmoidal nerves** (ethmoid sinuses, nasal cavity and, via the external nasal branch, the **tip of the nose**), and the **infratrochlear nerve**.

The **frontal** and **lacrimal** nerves pass through the superior orbital fissure **outside** the ring. The frontal nerve runs on top of the **levator palpebrae superioris** and divides into the **supraorbital** (through the supraorbital notch or foramen) and **supratrochlear** nerves.

V1 also sends a **tentorial (meningeal) branch** to the dura of the tentorium and falx, which helps explain why pain from dural structures can be felt behind the eye.

The **corneal (blink) reflex**: touching the cornea activates the nasociliary nerve (afferent, V1); signals reach the **spinal and principal trigeminal nuclei** in the brainstem, which connect to both **facial nuclei**; the facial nerve (efferent, VII) closes both eyes. Testing each eye separately tells you whether V1 or VII is at fault.

V1 also carries the afferent limb of the reflex tearing response, while the lacrimal gland's secretory fibers actually come from the **facial nerve** via the pterygopalatine ganglion and travel with branches of V2 and V1.
levels.phd:
The trigeminal ganglion is the cranial equivalent of a dorsal root ganglion: its **pseudounipolar** neurons, derived from both **neural crest** and **ectodermal placodes**, have one branch in the periphery and one in the brainstem. Corneal afferents are some of the densest sensory endings in the body, with roughly hundreds of terminals per square millimeter, and include **polymodal nociceptors** (TRPV1), **mechanonociceptors** (Piezo2) and **cold thermoreceptors** expressing **TRPM8**. Cold receptors fire continuously as tears evaporate and help regulate basal tear production and blinking; their dysfunction contributes to **dry eye** pain.

Central processing is spread along the brainstem: the **principal sensory nucleus** handles fine touch, the **spinal trigeminal nucleus** handles pain and temperature in an **onion-skin** pattern (perioral areas represented rostrally, outer face caudally), and the **mesencephalic nucleus** holds proprioceptive cell bodies inside the CNS, a unique arrangement.

The **trigeminovascular system** is central to migraine theory. V1 fibers innervate meningeal and cerebral vessels and release **CGRP** and substance P. Activation of these afferents and their second-order neurons in the **trigeminocervical complex** (spinal trigeminal nucleus plus upper cervical dorsal horns) can produce pain referred to the forehead and back of the head. This research led to drugs that block CGRP or its receptor, a major advance in migraine prevention.

The **trigeminal–autonomic reflex** links V1 input to parasympathetic output through the superior salivatory nucleus, explaining tearing and nasal congestion in **trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias** such as cluster headache.
levels.expert:
Testing V1: light touch and pinprick on the **forehead**, and the **corneal reflex** with a wisp of cotton. Sensory loss stops at the **midline** and at the **vertex** (C2 takes over behind it); a loss that extends across the angle of the jaw is not trigeminal, because that skin belongs to C2/C3.

**Herpes zoster ophthalmicus**: reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the V1 territory causes a painful vesicular rash on the forehead. **Hutchinson's sign**, vesicles on the tip of the nose, indicates **nasociliary** involvement and a high risk of eye involvement (keratitis, uveitis), so urgent ophthalmology review and antiviral treatment are needed.

**Trigeminal neuralgia** causes brief electric-shock pains, more often in V2/V3 than V1. Most cases come from **neurovascular compression** of the nerve root at the brainstem (often the superior cerebellar artery), seen on high-resolution MRI. In a young patient, consider **multiple sclerosis**. First-line treatment is medication; when that fails, **microvascular decompression** through a retrosigmoid craniotomy offers the most durable relief, with percutaneous procedures and **stereotactic radiosurgery** as alternatives.

**Neurotrophic keratopathy** follows loss of corneal sensation (after surgery, zoster or tumor): the numb cornea heals poorly and ulcerates. Lesions of the **cavernous sinus** or **superior orbital fissure** affect V1 along with CN III, IV and VI. **Raeder paratrigeminal syndrome** combines V1 pain with a postganglionic Horner syndrome.

During frontal craniotomies and **supraorbital keyhole** approaches, surgeons protect the supraorbital nerve to avoid forehead numbness.

keyPoints: V1 is the top, purely sensory branch of the trigeminal nerve
Runs in the cavernous sinus wall and enters the orbit via the superior orbital fissure
Carries the afferent limb of the corneal (blink) reflex; VII is the efferent
Hutchinson's sign (nose-tip zoster) warns of eye involvement

test.q: The corneal reflex has its afferent limb in which nerve?
test.explain: V1 senses the touch via the nasociliary nerve; VII closes the eyelids.

test.q: Name the three branches of V1 (one word each, the mnemonic).
Vesicles on the tip of the nose in shingles of the forehead suggest involvement of the:
test.explain: Hutchinson's sign: the external nasal branch comes from the nasociliary nerve, which also supplies the eye.

test.q: Sensory loss over the angle of the jaw is NOT trigeminal because that skin is supplied by:
test.explain: The angle of the jaw is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2–C3).

test.q: V1 enters the orbit through the superior orbital ______.
test.explain: The superior orbital fissure transmits CN III, IV, VI and the branches of V1.
